title: Valais and Dauphiné Early Trials: First Documentary Sabbath Charges
description:
The Alpine regions of Valais and Dauphiné in western Switzerland and southeastern France were the sites of the earliest well-documented prosecutions explicitly incorporating the concept of the witch sabbath. Beginning around 1419 and intensifying through the 1420s, secular and ecclesiastical courts in this region tried and executed hundreds of alleged witches on charges that included attendance at nocturnal assemblies (variously called synagogues, sabbaths, or sabbat), homage to the devil, infanticide, and ritual cannibalism. These Alpine trials are the earliest in which the full cumulative concept of witchcraft — combining traditional maleficium with diabolical pact and organized collective worship — appears in the documentary record.

The Valais trials produced a series of treatises in the 1430s that formalized the new concept of witchcraft, most notably Johannes Nider's Formicarius (c. 1435), which drew directly on information from the Alpine inquisitor Pierre of Bern. The geographic concentration of early trials in the Alpine arc — stretching from Savoy and Dauphiné through the Valais and into western Germany — suggests that the cumulative concept of witchcraft crystallized in a specific regional context before spreading throughout Europe.

Historians debate whether the Alpine trials represent the point of origin of the witch trials as a historical phenomenon or whether similar developments were occurring elsewhere simultaneously. The evidence for organized persecution is strongest in the Alpine region in this period, and the intellectual production of demonological theory in the 1430s–1450s draws explicitly on Alpine trial experience. The Valais trials thus represent both a historical watershed and a key site for understanding how the cumulative concept of witchcraft was constructed through judicial practice.
historiographical_note: Pierrette Paravy's De la Chrétienté romaine à la Réforme en Dauphiné (1993) provides the most thorough study of the early Alpine trials. Richard Kieckhefer's concept of the 'cumulative concept of witchcraft' — the merger of learned diabolism with popular maleficium — is particularly well illustrated by the Valais evidence. Martine Ostorero's work on the development of the sabbath concept emphasizes the Alpine origins of this crucial innovation.
source_method: Published trial records; notarial registers; secondary scholarship on the origins of witch persecution
